claim: Arabidopsis thaliana sepal development produces patterns of specialized cell types including giant cells interspersed between smaller cells.
source: During the development of Arabidopsis thaliana's outmost floral organ, the sepal, equivalent epidermal cells in the primordium differentiate to produce a scattered pattern of giant cells that are interspersed between smaller cells (Figure 1A–F; Roeder et al., 2010, 2012; Tauriello et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work (Roeder et al., 2010, 2012; Tauriello et al., 2015) and references to Figure 1A-F showing the pattern.

claim: Giant cells form when an epidermal cell undergoes multiple rounds of endoreduplication.
source: At maturity, giant cells are approximately one-fifth the length of the sepal and form when an epidermal cell undergoes multiple rounds of endoreduplication, an alternative cell cycle in which a cell replicates its DNA without undergoing mitotic division (Figure 1C–G; Roeder et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Roeder et al., 2010 and reference to Figure 1C-G.

claim: Mature sepals typically contain the same proportion of giant cells relative to small cells.
source: Mature sepals typically contain the same proportion of giant cells relative to small cells, although their spatial distribution varies from sepal to sepal and giant cells may even form adjacent to one another (Figure 1C–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1C-F showing variation in spatial distribution.

claim: The correct proportion of giant cells and small cells is needed to control the curvature of the sepal.
source: The correct proportion of giant cells and small cells is needed to control the curvature of the sepal; when the proportion of giant cells is altered, sepals are unable to enclose and protect the developing floral organs (Roeder et al., 2010, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Roeder et al., 2010, 2012.

claim: Giant cells do not form on the sepal epidermis in plants with loss-of-function mutations in ATML1.
source: We have previously shown that giant cells do not form on the sepal epidermis in plants with loss-of-function mutations in Arabidopsis thaliana MERISTEM LAYER1 (ATML1; Roeder et al., 2012), which encodes a class IV homeodomain-leucine zipper transcription factor (Lu et al., 1996; Nakamura et al., 2006; Schrick et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Roeder et al., 2012 and references describing ATML1 (Lu et al., 1996; Nakamura et al., 2006; Schrick et al., 2004).

claim: ATML1 is necessary for establishing the epidermal cell layer during early embryogenesis.
source: Previous research has indicated that ATML1 is necessary for establishing the epidermal cell layer during early embryogenesis (Lu et al., 1996; Roeder et al., 2012; Sessions et al., 1999; Takada and Jürgens, 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations (Lu et al., 1996; Roeder et al., 2012; Sessions et al., 1999; Takada and Jürgens, 2007).

claim: Plants doubly mutant for atml1 and its closely related paralog, protodermal factor 2, lack an epidermal layer and are seedling lethal.
source: Plants doubly mutant for atml1 and its closely related paralog, protodermal factor 2, lack an epidermal layer and are thus seedling lethal (Abe et al., 2003; Ogawa et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Abe et al., 2003 and Ogawa et al., 2015.

claim: Ectopic expression of ATML1 results in inappropriate differentiation of epidermal cell types in the inner cell layers of cotyledons.
source: Conversely, ectopic expression of ATML1 results in inappropriate differentiation of epidermal cell types in the inner cell layers of cotyledons (Peterson et al., 2013; Takada et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Peterson et al., 2013 and Takada et al., 2013.

claim: Expression of ATML1 can promote cells to adopt epidermal-specific cell identity in tissues other than the epidermis.
source: This result suggests that expression of ATML1 can promote cells to adopt epidermal-specific cell identity in tissues other than the epidermis.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the previous experimental result about ectopic ATML1 expression.

claim: ATML1 overexpression lines produced sepals almost entirely covered in giant cells.
source: ATML1 overexpression lines produced sepals almost entirely covered in giant cells (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 2A showing the phenotype.

claim: The proportion of highly endoreduplicated epidermal nuclei from ATML1 overexpression line sepals increased.
source: As expected, the proportion of highly endoreduplicated epidermal nuclei from ATML1 overexpression line sepals increased (Figure 2I, red bars).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 2I showing flow cytometry data.

claim: ATML1 overexpression line sepals contained a greater proportion of 16C and 32C giant cells than wild type.
source: These sepals contained a greater proportion of 16C and 32C giant cells than wild type, and on occasion a few cells even underwent an additional endocycle (64C; Figure 2I, red bars).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 2I showing ploidy distribution.

claim: In ATML1 overexpression line sepals, the giant cell marker was expressed in almost every epidermal cell and the small cell marker was expressed only in a few remaining small cells.
source: In these crossed sepals, the giant cell marker was expressed in almost every epidermal cell and the small cell marker was expressed only in a few remaining small cells (Figure 2J and K).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 2J and K showing marker expression.

claim: Ectopic giant cells formed on the sepal five days after being treated with 10 µM estradiol in an ATML1 estradiol-inducible line.
source: To validate that ATML1 alone is sufficient to drive giant cell formation, we induced ATML1 expression in inflorescences using an ATML1 estradiol-inducible line. Ectopic giant cells formed on the sepal five days after being treated with 10 µM estradiol (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 1 showing the induction experiment.

claim: High levels of ATML1 are sufficient to induce sepal epidermal cells to adopt giant cell identity and can force a deterministic all-giant cell pattern.
source: Overall, these results suggest that high levels of ATML1 are sufficient to induce sepal epidermal cells to adopt giant cell identity and can force a deterministic all-giant cell pattern.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the overexpression and induction experiments.

claim: ATML1 influences giant cell formation in a dosage-dependent manner, where the amount of ATML1 expressed will determine the proportion of giant cells that form in the sepal.
source: Together, these results suggest that ATML1 influences giant cell formation in a dosage-dependent manner, where the amount of ATML1 expressed will determine the proportion of giant cells that form in the sepal.
evidence: The claim is supported by the genetic dosage series experiments showing correlation between ATML1 levels and giant cell numbers (Figure 2).

claim: The mCitrine-ATML1 fusion protein functions similarly to endogenous ATML1.
source: We recovered two independent transgenic lines that fully rescue the atml1–3 loss-of-giant cell mutant phenotype (Figure 3A–D; Materials and methods). Both lines exhibited similar behavior, thus we focused our analysis on one of them. Overall, these results suggest that our mCitrine-ATML1 fusion protein functions similarly to endogenous ATML1 (Figure 1C–F; Figure 3A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by the rescue experiment shown in Figure 3A-D.

claim: In the developing sepal, mean normalized mCitrine-ATML1 concentrations differ between individual nuclei.
source: We observed that in the developing sepal, mean normalized mCitrine-ATML1 concentrations differ between individual nuclei (Figure 3G–J; sepals show a mean coefficient of variation (CV) of approximately 0.2).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification shown in Figure 3G-J.

claim: In the floral meristem, which does not form giant cells, mCitrine-ATML1 concentrations are more uniform.
source: Conversely in the floral meristem, which does not form giant cells, mCitrine-ATML1 concentrations are more uniform (Figure 3E–F and I–J; meristems show a mean CV of approximately 0.1).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification shown in Figure 3E-F and I-J.

claim: The distribution of ATML1 concentrations in individual nuclei is broader in the sepal than in the meristem.
source: In particular, we can see that although unimodal, the distribution of ATML1 concentrations in individual nuclei is broader in the sepal than in the meristem, both for lower and higher values (Figure 3J).
evidence: The claim is supported by the histogram in Figure 3J.

claim: mCitrine-ATML1 concentrations in the sepal were approximately twice as variable as VIP1-mCitrine, AP2-2XYpet, and SEC24A reporters.
source: We found that mCitrine-ATML1 concentrations in the sepal were approximately twice as variable as the other reporters (Figure 3I, Figure 3—figure supplement 1; VIP1 sepals show a mean CV of approximately 0.12; AP2 sepals show a mean CV of approximately 0.14; SEC24A sepals show a mean CV of approximately 0.12), suggesting that varying expression levels in sepal epidermal cells is not a common feature observed for every gene.
evidence: The claim is supported by CV comparisons shown in Figure 3I and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: During early sepal development, epidermal cells not only have varying amounts of mCitrine-ATML1, but also that mCitrine-ATML1 levels fluctuate within individual cells over time.
source: We found that during early sepal development, epidermal cells not only have varying amounts of mCitrine-ATML1, but also that mCitrine-ATML1 levels fluctuate within individual cells over time (Figure 4A–C; Figure 4—figure supplements 1A–C; 2A–C; and 3A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by live imaging time series shown in Figure 4 and supplements.

claim: Cells that eventually become giant generally exhibit fluctuations reaching higher concentrations of mCitrine-ATML1 before endoreduplication initiates than cells that mitotically divide.
source: We observed that cells that eventually become giant generally exhibit fluctuations reaching higher concentrations of mCitrine-ATML1 before endoreduplication initiates than cells that mitotically divide.
evidence: The claim is based on tracking mCitrine-ATML1 levels in cells with different fates during live imaging.

claim: ATML1 concentration peaks have predictive power in discriminating small versus giant cell fate with an average AUC of 0.74.
source: We observed an average AUC of 0.74 in our different datasets, highlighting the predictive power of ATML1 concentration peaks in discriminating small versus giant cell fate (AUC = 0.76, 0.69, 0.73, 0.78; Figure 4E; Figure 4—figure supplements 1E, 2E and 3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by ROC analysis shown in Figure 4E and supplements.

claim: The heterogeneity in ATML1 among cells in the sepal primordium can be explained by dynamic cell-autonomous fluctuations.
source: In summary, we show that the heterogeneity in ATML1 among cells in the sepal primordium can be explained by dynamic cell-autonomous fluctuations, where giant and small cell fate are strongly correlated with the concentration of ATML1 reached.
evidence: The claim is a summary inference from the live imaging and quantification data.

claim: Cells with high concentration fluctuations of ATML1 will likely endoreduplicate and become giant, whereas cells with low concentration fluctuations will likely go on to divide and remain small.
source: Cells with high concentration fluctuations of ATML1 will likely endoreduplicate and become giant, whereas cells with low concentration fluctuations will likely go on to divide and remain small.
evidence: The claim is a summary of the correlation between ATML1 levels and cell fate.

claim: Both small cells and giant cells show similar peak levels of mCitrine-ATML1 in 2C (G1 phase).
source: We found that in the preceding cell cycle, both small cells and giant cells show similar peak levels of mCitrine-ATML1 in 2C (Figure 4F; Figure 4—figure supplements 1F, 2F and 3F).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4F and supplements.

claim: ATML1 concentration peaks during the G1 (2C) stage are not predictive of cell fate.
source: Our ROC analysis shows that ATML1 concentration peaks during the G1 (2C) stage are not predictive of cell fate (AUCs = 0.54, 0.37, 0.43, 0.37; Figure 4G; Figure 4—figure supplements 1G, 2G and 3G).
evidence: The claim is supported by ROC analysis shown in Figure 4G and supplements.

claim: Most cells that experience relatively high peak concentrations of mCitrine-ATML1 while in 4C endoreduplicate and become giant cells.
source: In contrast, most cells that experience relatively high peak concentrations of mCitrine-ATML1 while in 4C endoreduplicate and become giant cells (Figure 4H,J–Q; Figure 4—figure supplements 1H,J–Q, 2H,J–O and 3H,J–Q).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4H and related panels.

claim: ATML1 concentration peaks in 4C are strongly predictive of cell fate.
source: Our ROC analysis is consistent with this observation, showing that ATML1 concentration peaks in 4C are strongly predictive of cell fate (AUCs = 0.80, 0.80, 0.80, 0.84; Figure 4I; Figure 4—figure supplements 1I, 2I and 3I).
evidence: The claim is supported by ROC analysis shown in Figure 4I and supplements.

claim: A cell is competent to respond to high levels of ATML1 mainly during G2 to induce giant cell formation.
source: Overall, these results suggest that a cell is competent to respond to high levels of ATML1 mainly during G2 to induce giant cell formation.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the G2-specific predictive power of ATML1 levels.

claim: Almost all endoreduplicating cells in pPDF1::GFP-ATML1 sepals exhibited high peak levels of GFP-ATML1 in G2, above the common threshold.
source: Applying this threshold to the pPDF1::GFP-ATML1 data, we observed that almost all endoreduplicating cells exhibited high peak levels of GFP-ATML1 in G2, above the common threshold (Figure 5D–J; Figure 5—figure supplements 1C–F; and 2C–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5D-J and supplements.

claim: The overexpression line follows the same threshold-based cell-autonomous fluctuation patterning mechanism.
source: Combined, these data suggest that our overexpression line follows the same threshold-based cell-autonomous fluctuation patterning mechanism; the increased basal GFP-ATML1 expression from the PDF1 promoter raises ATML1 production levels such that almost all sepal epidermal cells surpass the giant cell fate-inducing threshold during G2.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the overexpression data and threshold analysis.

claim: LGO acts genetically downstream of ATML1 to establish giant cells.
source: To verify that LGO acts genetically downstream of ATML1 to establish giant cells, we crossed our ATML1 overexpression line (pPDF1::FLAG-ATML1) to our lgo-2 mutant, which exhibits a loss-of-giant cell phenotype (Figure 6C). Plants homozygous for both the lgo-2 mutation and the overexpression transgene do not form giant cells, demonstrating that LGO activity is required downstream of ATML1 for formation of giant cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by genetic epistasis analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: ATML1 fluctuates independently of LGO.
source: These plants still exhibited mCitrine-ATML1 fluctuations, suggesting that ATML1 fluctuates independently of LGO (Figure 6B,E–J; Figure 6—figure supplements 1B–F; and 2B–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by live imaging of lgo mutants shown in Figure 6 and supplements.

claim: There are no significant differences between the predicted number of giant cells in the lgo-2 mutant and the observed number of giant cells in wild type.
source: We found no significant differences between the predicted number of giant cells in the lgo-2 mutant and the observed number of giant cells in wild type (Figure 6D–F; Figure 6—figure supplements 1C–D and 2C–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification shown in Figure 6D-F and supplements.

claim: A cell may still fluctuate to high levels of ATML1 in G2 but without LGO, cells cannot respond to these fluctuations to trigger endoreduplication.
source: This suggests that a cell may still fluctuate to high levels of ATML1 in G2 but without LGO, cells cannot respond to these fluctuations to trigger endoreduplication.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the lgo mutant analysis.

claim: ATML1 fluctuations are independent of endoreduplication.
source: Since the absence of LGO does not seem to change the dynamics of ATML1, this result further indicates that ATML1 fluctuations are independent of endoreduplication.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the observation that ATML1 fluctuates normally in lgo mutants.

claim: A simple computational model that exhibits cell-autonomous stochastic fluctuations of ATML1 is sufficient to recapitulate giant cell patterning.
source: We therefore asked whether a simple computational model that exhibits cell-autonomous stochastic fluctuations of ATML1 is sufficient to recapitulate giant cell patterning as observed in our experimental data.
evidence: The claim is tested through computational modeling described in the manuscript.

claim: The model qualitatively reproduced experimental data and led to a scattered pattern of giant cells in a growing tissue.
source: The model qualitatively reproduced our experimental data and led to a scattered pattern of giant cells in a growing tissue (Figure 7B, Video 11).
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 7B and Video 11.

claim: Dynamic fluctuations in ATML1 and in the target during G2 enable a subset of cells from the developing tissue to become giant cells.
source: Specifically, dynamic fluctuations in ATML1 and in the target during G2 enable a subset of cells from the developing tissue to become giant cells (Figure 7C–E; Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 7C-E and supplement.

claim: The model found parameter values that produced wild-type-like sepals, in which the distributions of ATML1 levels and the number of giant cells were similar to those observed experimentally.
source: We found parameter values that produced wild-type-like sepals, in which the distributions of ATML1 levels and the number of giant cells were similar to those observed experimentally (Figures 3I–J and 7D; Materials and methods).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of simulation and experimental data in Figures 3I-J and 7D.

claim: Lowering the intensity of the stochastic fluctuations in the model prevented it from matching the experimental data.
source: Furthermore, lowering the intensity of the stochastic fluctuations in the model prevented it from matching the experimental data (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by parameter exploration shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: The model shows lower AUC values in 2C stages than in 4C, consistent with experimental observations.
source: Consistent with our experimental observations, we found lower AUC values in 2C stages than in 4C.
evidence: The claim is supported by ROC analysis of simulated data.

claim: ATML1 levels during the G2 phase of the cell cycle are important for giant cell fate commitment.
source: This supports our hypothesis that ATML1 levels during the G2 phase of the cell cycle are important for giant cell fate commitment (Figure 7F–G and Figure 7—figure supplement 3A–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by model analysis shown in Figure 7F-G and supplement.

claim: With no feedback or low feedback strengths, the model could qualitatively match the experimental ROC analysis.
source: With no feedback or low feedback strengths, we could qualitatively match the experimental ROC analysis (Figure 7—figure supplements 3K–N; and 4A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by parameter exploration shown in Figure 7—figure supplements 3K-N and 4A-B.

claim: High feedback strengths lead to bistability in the system, inducing large and slow fluctuations between high and low levels.
source: Higher feedback strengths lead to bistability in the system, inducing large and slow fluctuations between high and low levels (Figure 7—figure supplement 4C–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 4C-D.

claim: ATML1 induction with 10 µM estradiol lead to total ATML1 levels 7.1 times higher than the mock treated samples, and increased endogenous ATML1 expression 1.5-fold within 48 hr.
source: We found that ATML1 induction with 10 µM estradiol lead to total ATML1 levels 7.1 times higher than the mock treated samples, and increased endogenous ATML1 expression 1.5-fold within 48 hr (Figure 7—figure supplement 4E–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 4E-F.

claim: The feedback of ATML1 on itself is not activating ATML1 further than other targets at the 48 hr time point.
source: This level of induction was similar to that observed in other downstream genes, suggesting that the feedback of ATML1 on itself is not activating ATML1 further than other targets at the 48 hr time point (Figure 7—figure supplement 4E–F).
evidence: The claim is an inference from comparing ATML1 induction to other downstream genes shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 4E-F.

claim: Changing the basal ATML1 production rate was sufficient to gradually increase the total amount of the ATML1 in the modeled tissue, and accordingly, the fraction of giant cells in the sepal.
source: We found that changing the basal ATML1 production rate was sufficient to gradually increase the total amount of the ATML1 in the modeled tissue, and accordingly, the fraction of giant cells in the sepal (Figure 8).
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 8.

claim: There is a positive relationship between graded ATML1 levels and the fraction of giant cells produced in the tissue.
source: These results, together with our dosage analysis, show that there is a positive relationship between graded ATML1 levels and the fraction of giant cells produced in the tissue (Figures 2 and 8).
evidence: The claim is supported by both experimental (Figure 2) and simulation (Figure 8) data.

claim: Fast and relatively small stochastic fluctuations of ATML1 are sufficient to pattern giant and small cells in the sepal.
source: Hence, our model shows that fast and relatively small stochastic fluctuations of ATML1 are sufficient to pattern giant and small cells in the sepal.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion from the modeling work.

claim: ATML1 activates a downstream target, which if activated in G2, will induce endoreduplication.
source: ATML1 activates a downstream target, which if activated in G2, will induce endoreduplication.
evidence: The claim is part of the model framework.

claim: The dynamics of the ATML1-target network creates a soft ATML1 threshold during G2.
source: The dynamics of the ATML1-target network creates a soft ATML1 threshold during G2.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion from the modeling work.

claim: During Arabidopsis sepal development, the pattern of giant cells and small cells in the epidermis is initiated through fluctuations of the transcription factor ATML1.
source: Here, we have identified a cell-autonomous fluctuation patterning mechanism for specifying cell fate in a multicellular system (Figure 9). During Arabidopsis sepal development, the pattern of giant cells and small cells in the epidermis is initiated through fluctuations of the transcription factor ATML1.
evidence: The claim is the main conclusion of the study, supported by all the experimental and modeling data.

claim: Cells in which ATML1 levels surpass a soft threshold during the G2 phase of the cell cycle have a high probability of establishing giant cell identity and entering endoreduplication.
source: Using live-imaging, quantitative image analyses and mathematical modeling, we have revealed that cells in which ATML1 levels surpass a soft threshold during the G2 phase of the cell cycle have a high probability of establishing giant cell identity and entering endoreduplication.
evidence: The claim is a main conclusion supported by live imaging, quantification, and modeling.

claim: A sepal epidermal cell is only competent to respond to ATML1 fluctuations during a window of time defined by G2 stage of the cell cycle.
source: A sepal epidermal cell is only competent to respond to ATML1 fluctuations during a window of time defined by G2 stage of the cell cycle.
evidence: The claim is a main conclusion supported by the G2-specific predictive power of ATML1 levels.

claim: The fluctuation-patterning model resembles Wolpert's French flag model in that each individual cell makes an autonomous fate decision based on the concentration of a key developmental regulator.
source: Strikingly, our fluctuation-patterning model resembles Wolpert's French flag model in that each individual cell makes an autonomous fate decision based on the concentration of a key developmental regulator.
evidence: The claim is a comparison to an established model in developmental biology.

claim: The fluctuation-patterning model deviates from the French flag model because it utilizes internal fluctuations instead of a diffusible morphogen to generate concentration differences.
source: Our model however deviates from the French flag model because it utilizes internal fluctuations instead of a diffusible morphogen to generate concentration differences.
evidence: The claim is a comparison highlighting the novelty of the mechanism.

claim: Giant cell formation is highly responsive to changes in the basal production of ATML1.
source: This sensitivity to small changes in concentration is consistent with our results in the sepal, where giant cell formation is highly responsive to changes in the basal production of ATML1.
evidence: The claim is supported by the dosage series experiments.

claim: In wild-type plants, the number of giant cells varies only slightly from sepal to sepal, falling within a small range (10-30).
source: Interestingly however, in wild-type plants, the number of giant cells varies only slightly from sepal to sepal, falling within a small range (10-30).
evidence: The claim is based on observation of wild-type sepals.

claim: These fluctuations together with a threshold must be tuned to ensure that the correct proportion of giant cells form on the sepal.
source: This indicates that these fluctuations together with a threshold must be tuned to ensure that the correct proportion of giant cells form on the sepal.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the observation of consistent giant cell proportions.

claim: The cell cycle acts as a stabilizing factor to restrict giant cell fate decisions.
source: Our data suggests that the cell cycle acts as a stabilizing factor to restrict giant cell fate decisions similarly to secondary mechanisms used in other biological systems.
evidence: The claim is an inference from the G2-specific competence for giant cell fate.

claim: LGO is a Siamese-related CDK inhibitor that acts genetically downstream of ATML1 in the giant cell pathway to promote endoreduplication once giant cell identity is acquired.
source: One possible ATML1 target is the Siamese-related CDK inhibitor LGO. LGO acts genetically downstream of ATML1 in the giant cell pathway to promote endoreduplication once giant cell identity is acquired (Figure 6C; Roeder et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by genetic epistasis data (Figure 6C) and citation to Roeder et al., 2012.

claim: ACR4 acts upstream of ATML1 during giant cell formation.
source: An epistasis analysis between ACR4, DEK1 and ATML1 reveals that during giant cell formation, ACR4 acts upstream of ATML1 but that DEK1 acts downstream (Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by genetic epistasis data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claim: DEK1 acts downstream of ATML1 during giant cell formation.
source: An epistasis analysis between ACR4, DEK1 and ATML1 reveals that during giant cell formation, ACR4 acts upstream of ATML1 but that DEK1 acts downstream (Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by genetic epistasis data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1.
